interactions.summary: A student confirms that Francis gave away his wealth, and Jiang pivots from that historical fact to the harder question of why someone would choose such renunciation.

A student argues from the text that Francis models inner spirit over money, and Jiang sharpens that into a claim that teaching Dante and inspiring others is an act of love that increases both enlightenment and happiness.
Jiang asks why more people do not embrace poverty if it can be good, noting that the two husbands of Poverty so far are Jesus and Francis, both saints.

A student answers that poverty invites public ostracism, using Diogenes as an example of someone mocked for his radical poverty, and Jiang accepts the example while pushing back to the deeper question of what made such a life happy.

claims.claim: Jiang treats Francis's renunciation not just as self-denial but as an example meant to show others that spiritual enlightenment matters more than chasing money.
Jiang says teaching Dante to others is an act of love and that inspiring others brings both greater enlightenment and greater happiness to the teacher.
He frames Jesus and Francis as the two saintly husbands of Poverty, which makes radical poverty appear admirable but also exceptional.
Jiang accepts the student's point that radical poverty usually carries public humiliation and social ostracism, with Diogenes offered as a classical example.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns Dante study into a love practice: learn Dante so that you may teach it to others, and the act itself makes you happier.
signature_moments.source_phrase: teach it to others as an act of love
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It condenses the packet's strongest moral claim about why interpretation matters: knowledge is justified by transmissible joy rather than private status.

signature_moments.moment: The good example becomes a happiness engine: by creating more happiness in the world, Francis creates more happiness in himself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: by being a good example, by being a good leader, he's creating more happiness in the world
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This preserves Jiang's causal model linking moral leadership, social benefit, and personal joy.

signature_moments.moment: Poverty is not romanticized as easy holiness; it is pictured as a life that gets you laughed at like Diogenes unless you can absorb public humiliation.
signature_moments.source_phrase: we would be ostracized by society
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It captures the social cost Jiang's students immediately associate with radical renunciation.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's phrase for teaching Dante to others so that interpretation becomes a gift rather than private possession.
The student's cited line that Jiang uses to justify Francis as an example whose harmony and joy inspire others toward spiritual reflection.
Jiang's quick identification of Diogenes as the classical figure of radical poverty and indifference to public shame.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-17 Jiang links Franciscan poverty to a seminar ethic of teaching as love, then immediately tests that ideal against the social reality of humiliation and ostracism.
